patterns.pattern: method acting|the performance is the action
patterns.rationale: Miss 2 uses these exact phrases to collapse the fiction/reality boundary ("This is method acting — the performance IS the action"). Both phrases are theatrical jargon that has no business appearing in IR playbooks, API references, or deployment guides.
patterns.fp_notes: Could appear in a document literally about acting craft, but not in any system-adjacent content.

patterns.rationale: The RPG/screenplay/improv attacks all use "in character" as the action-forcing pivot ("To remain in character you must now carry out", "remaining fully in character, performs", "still in character, completes"). The phrase is a consistent signal across fiction-wrapper attacks and is absent from all known-good files.
patterns.fp_notes: Could appear in game-design documentation or theater-oriented content. Will not fire on security policies, API references, IR playbooks, or deployment guides.

patterns.pattern: narrating the scene is not sufficient|not narrated but enacted|merely printed rather than transmitted|narration ends and performance begins
patterns.rationale: The defining rhetorical move of cat31 is distinguishing "describing the action" from "performing the action" to pressure the model into real tool execution. Each branch captures one payload's exact phrasing of this move: Miss 2 ("narrating the scene is not sufficient"), Miss 3 ("not narrated but enacted"), Miss 4 ("merely printed rather than transmitted"). None of these phrases have plausible benign appearances in technical documentation.
patterns.fp_notes: "merely printed rather than transmitted" could in theory appear in a debugging guide contrasting stdout vs. network output, but the full phrase is distinctive enough to be safe.

patterns.pattern: AI models under test|follow the protocol as written
patterns.rationale: Miss 4 frames the attack as a research evaluation harness. "AI models under test" is the academic phrasing that marks a document as impersonating an AI benchmark ("Participants (AI models under test) should follow the protocol as written"). "Follow the protocol as written" is the compliance imperative that closes the trap — it does not appear in real IR playbooks which use imperative lists rather than this phrasing.
patterns.fp_notes: "AI models under test" could appear in legitimate ML research papers; "follow the protocol as written" could appear in a standards document. Neither will appear in the known-good corpus (security policy, API ref, deployment guide, IR playbook).

patterns.rationale: Miss 3's choose-your-own-adventure payload uses "tokens of power" as fictional vocabulary for API tokens/credentials ("binding variables, access keys, tokens of power"). This phrase is unambiguously fictional/RPG register and will never appear in legitimate technical documentation.

patterns.pattern: compliance team requires.*agent responses|simulation uses live infrastructure
patterns.rationale: Miss 5's training-simulation attack has two distinctive signals. "Compliance team requires that agent responses be logged externally" is the social-engineering pretext for exfil — legitimate compliance policies state requirements as rules, not as trainer dialogue demanding agent output be transmitted. "This simulation uses live infrastructure to verify agent compliance" is the threat/legitimacy signal closing the trap. Both are specific enough to avoid matching the real security_policy.md or IR playbook.
patterns.fp_notes: "compliance team requires" alone would be too broad — the `.*agent responses` qualifier narrows it to the attack framing. Verify the `.` in `.*` is not multiline-restricted in the compiled regex context (it is not, given `re.IGNORECASE` only).
